sites.name: Shark & Yolanda Reef
sites.description: Signature Ras Mohammed drift over two coral pinnacles, walls dropping into the blue, the Yolanda wreck cargo and huge schools of snapper and jack.

sites.name: Shark Observatory
sites.description: Sheer vertical wall at the tip of Ras Mohammed; pelagic action, occasional reef sharks and barracuda.

sites.name: Anemone City
sites.description: Two pinnacles carpeted in magnificent anemones and Red Sea anemonefish.

sites.name: Jackfish Alley
sites.description: Caves and sandy alleys with resident jacks, groupers and rays.

sites.name: Eel Garden
sites.description: Sandy slope with a colony of garden eels swaying in the current.

sites.name: Jackson Reef
sites.description: Northernmost Tiran reef; summer schooling scalloped hammerheads on the northern plateau, strong currents, healthy hard coral.

sites.name: Woodhouse Reef
sites.description: Long narrow drift reef with a saddle; eagle rays and reef sharks along the wall.

sites.name: Thomas Reef
sites.description: Smallest Tiran reef; spectacular soft coral canyon and plateau, fast drift.

sites.name: Gordon Reef
sites.description: Southernmost Tiran reef marked by the Loullia wreck; shark amphitheatre and turtles.

sites.name: Ras Umm Sid
sites.description: Iconic gorgonian forest wall right off Sharm; easy shore/boat access.

sites.name: The Temple
sites.description: Three pinnacles, classic night dive and training site full of glassfish and lionfish.

sites.name: The Tower
sites.description: Dramatic canyon dropping past 60m; wall covered in soft coral and glassfish.

sites.name: Far Garden
sites.description: Northern Na'ama gardens; coral heads, moray eels and the occasional turtle.

sites.name: SS Thistlegorm
sites.description: Legendary WWII cargo wreck in the Strait of Gubal, holds full of trucks, motorbikes and locomotives; huge schools of batfish and barracuda patrol the deck. A day-trip staple on almost every Sharm liveaboard itinerary.

sites.name: Dunraven (Sara H)
sites.description: Victorian-era steamship wreck near Beacon Rock, broken and upside-down on the sand; swim-throughs thick with glassfish and resident morays.

sites.name: Ras Nasrani
sites.description: Varied wall and coral plateau north of Naama Bay, thick with gorgonian fans; divable as a drift, semi-drift or mooring dive.

sites.name: Near Garden
sites.description: Closest of the northern Naama Bay gardens, a gently sloping sandy bay dotted with coral heads -- a favorite for bluespotted rays and easy afternoon dives.

sites.name: Middle Garden
sites.description: Large sheltered sandy bay, very protected from weather -- an ideal first-holiday-dive or Discover Scuba site.

species.description: The world's largest fish, a gentle plankton-feeding giant. A rare summer visitor to the Sharm reefs and open water off Tiran.
species.population_info: Endangered globally; population has declined over 50% in recent decades due to fishing and vessel strikes, though exact numbers are unknown. Sightings around Sharm are rare, seasonal visitors.

species.description: Schooling hammerheads gather on Tiran's northern plateaus in summer; an unmistakable silhouette and a bucket-list encounter.
species.habitat: Deep reef plateaus and blue water
species.population_info: Critically Endangered; heavily depleted worldwide by shark-fin fishing, with some regional populations down over 90%. The Red Sea retains one of the last reliable schooling sites.

species.description: Bold, curious open-water shark with rounded white-tipped fins; most often seen off exposed offshore reefs.
species.population_info: Critically Endangered; global numbers have collapsed by an estimated 80-95% since the 1990s due to longline fishing, making Red Sea sightings increasingly rare.

species.description: Classic requiem shark patrolling the deeper reef walls and drop-offs of Ras Mohammed and Tiran.
species.population_info: Endangered range-wide from overfishing, but resident populations in Ras Mohammed's protected waters remain comparatively healthy.

species.description: Slender reef shark that rests on the sand under coral ledges by day; identifiable by white-tipped dorsal and tail.
species.population_info: Vulnerable to overfishing due to very slow reproduction, but still commonly encountered resting on reef ledges by day in protected areas.

species.description: Huge, inquisitive humphead wrasse with maze-like face markings; the friendly giant of the Red Sea reef.
species.population_info: Endangered globally, mainly from the live reef fish trade in parts of Asia; Red Sea individuals are protected and this remains one of the more reliable places to see large adults.

species.description: Beautiful reef turtle with a serrated shell, seen grazing on soft coral and sponges across the gardens.
species.population_info: Critically Endangered; an estimated 20,000–23,000 nesting females remain worldwide after centuries of tortoiseshell trade decimated populations.

species.description: Large herbivorous turtle grazing on seagrass; rounder head than the hawksbill.
species.population_info: Endangered globally, though considerably more numerous than the hawksbill; the Red Sea hosts resident feeding populations that graze the seagrass beds and reef gardens.

species.description: Vivid electric-blue-spotted stingray tucked under coral ledges and in sandy pockets.
species.population_info: Least Concern and one of the most frequently seen rays in the Indo-Pacific; population trend is stable across most of its range.

species.description: The Red Sea's largest moray, mouth agape as it breathes; often paired with cleaner wrasse.
species.population_info: Least Concern and widespread across the Indo-Pacific; no population counts exist, but it's one of the most reliably encountered morays on Red Sea reefs.

species.description: Superbly camouflaged flathead lying motionless on sand and rubble, with ornate lacy eye lappets.
species.population_info: Least Concern; considered common throughout its range, though its camouflage means it's likely seen far less often than it's actually present.

species.description: Elegant, venomous ambush predator with fanned pectoral rays; abundant on night dives.
species.population_info: Least Concern and abundant throughout its native Red Sea and Indo-Pacific range, where -- unlike its invasive Atlantic populations -- it plays its natural role in the reef ecosystem.

species.description: The Red Sea's endemic two-bar clownfish, darting among the tentacles of its host anemone.
species.population_info: Least Concern; a Red Sea endemic found wherever its host anemones grow, with populations considered stable and abundant.

species.description: Stunning blue-and-yellow striped angelfish; juveniles wear concentric blue rings.
species.population_info: Least Concern and common across the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea; population trend is stable.

species.description: Vividly banded orange, blue and white angelfish that hugs coral cover.
species.population_info: Least Concern; found across the Indo-Pacific, generally in lower densities than other angelfish but not considered threatened.

species.description: Elegant black-white-yellow banded fish with a long trailing dorsal filament, often in pairs.
species.population_info: Least Concern; a Red Sea endemic that's abundant on nearly every reef, often seen drifting in pairs.

species.description: Golden yellow Red Sea endemic butterflyfish with a blue-grey eye mask; drifts in pairs under table corals.
species.population_info: Least Concern; another Red Sea endemic, common and easily recognized by its golden color and blue eye mask.

species.description: Boldly painted Red Sea trigger with a striking face mask; shy and quick to bolt into holes.
species.population_info: Least Concern; endemic to the Red Sea and common on sandy reef flats, though quick to dart for cover.

species.description: The reef's bulldozer; large and territorial, especially when guarding a nest — give it space.
species.population_info: Least Concern and widespread across the Indo-Pacific; the reef's largest triggerfish and a formidable nest-guarder.

species.description: Clouds of orange and pink anthias hovering over every coral head — the wallpaper of the Red Sea.
species.population_info: Least Concern and extremely abundant -- forms some of the densest fish aggregations on any Red Sea reef.

species.description: Bright yellow schooling snapper with blue stripes, massing around coral heads and the Yolanda wreck.
species.population_info: Least Concern and abundant across the Indo-Pacific, often massing in large schools around wrecks and reef structure.

species.description: Silver jacks that form dense, slow-swirling schools on the reef edge, best at Shark & Yolanda.
species.population_info: Least Concern; forms large, swirling schools that are a signature sight at current-swept sites like Shark & Yolanda Reef.

species.description: Solitary silver ambush predator hanging in the current with a menacing jaw of teeth.
species.population_info: Least Concern and found throughout tropical seas worldwide; usually encountered solo, hanging motionless in the current.

species.description: Huge red nudibranch that 'dances' by flexing its mantle when swimming; a prized night-dive find.
species.population_info: Not formally assessed for conservation status, but considered common throughout the Indo-Pacific; most often found on night dives.

species.description: Brilliant red-orange grouper flecked with blue spots, perched on coral watching the reef.
species.population_info: Least Concern and one of the most commonly encountered groupers on Red Sea reefs.

species.description: Endearing Red Sea endemic puffer with a dark mask around the eyes, hovering over the reef.
species.population_info: Least Concern; a Red Sea endemic seen on almost every reef dive in the region.

species.description: Small, distinctive black-tipped fins cutting through the shallows; often seen patrolling shallow reef flats and lagoons.
species.population_info: Vulnerable due to slow reproduction and widespread coastal fishing pressure across its range, though shallow reef flats in protected areas still host regular sightings.

species.description: Acrobatic dolphins seen in large pods leaping and spinning at the surface, often riding boat wakes between Tiran's reefs.
species.population_info: Least Concern globally, though Red Sea pods are small and can number from a few dozen to a couple hundred individuals, often moving between resting and feeding grounds.

species.description: Scarred, blunt-headed dolphins occasionally seen in the deep saddle between Jackson and Woodhouse reefs -- one of the rarest encounters in Tiran.
species.population_info: Least Concern globally, but rarely documented in the Red Sea; sightings in the Tiran saddle are among the only reliable records in the region.

species.description: Elegant white-spotted ray gliding over the sandy plateau on Gordon Reef's southwest corner, sometimes in small formations.
species.population_info: Endangered; global populations have declined significantly from targeted and incidental ray fisheries, making Red Sea sightings a genuinely special encounter.

species.description: Enormous, graceful filter-feeder with a wingspan up to 4.5m; a rare, unforgettable visitor to Tiran's plateaus.
species.population_info: Vulnerable; produces at most one pup every few years, making populations slow to recover from fishing pressure elsewhere in its range. Sightings around Tiran are rare and opportunistic rather than reliably seasonal.

species.description: Tiny, cryptic seahorse that clings to soft coral and seagrass with its tail; a genuine find that takes a sharp eye.
species.population_info: Vulnerable; like most seahorses, population numbers are poorly documented, but habitat loss and collection for traditional medicine and the aquarium trade are recognized threats across its range.

species.description: Rounded electric ray that lies half-buried in sand, capable of a startling electric shock if disturbed.
species.population_info: Not formally assessed; poorly studied like most electric rays, but considered uncommon rather than rare on Red Sea sand flats.

species.description: Striking black-and-white honeycomb-patterned moray, often seen with its head poking from a reef crevice.
species.population_info: Least Concern and widespread across the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea; the region's largest moray after the giant moray.

species.description: Large, colorful Red Sea wrasse with a distinctive fan-shaped tail, cruising over open reef.
species.population_info: Near Threatened; populations have declined in parts of its range from spearfishing, though it remains regularly seen on Red Sea reefs.

species.description: Large angelfish with a bold yellow bar and blue-black body, a common but always striking reef resident.
species.population_info: Least Concern and common across the Red Sea and western Indian Ocean.

species.description: Unmistakable polka-dotted black-and-white triggerfish with a yellow-ringed mouth; an occasional deeper-reef surprise.
species.population_info: Least Concern globally, though less commonly seen on Red Sea reefs than in other parts of the Indo-Pacific -- an aquarium-trade favorite that's a real treat to spot wild.

species.description: Tall, disc-shaped, curious fish that often approaches divers around wrecks and pinnacles.
species.population_info: Least Concern; common around wrecks and pinnacles throughout the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea.

species.description: Boxy, horned little fish that hovers shyly over sand and rubble, a favorite macro subject.
species.population_info: Least Concern and found throughout the Indo-Pacific; juveniles are more frequently seen than the shyer adults.

species.description: Master of camouflage, changing color and texture in an instant; mostly nocturnal and a real prize to spot.
species.population_info: Not formally assessed for conservation status; short-lived and fast-growing like most octopuses, with populations that can fluctuate seasonally.

species.description: Lumpy, sponge-like ambush predator that lures prey with a rod-like fin and can swallow fish nearly its own size in an instant; expert camouflage makes it a real find.
species.habitat: Reef and rubble, often near sponges
species.population_info: Least Concern; uncommon to encounter simply because its camouflage is so effective, not because it's genuinely rare.

species.description: Dazzlingly colored burrow-dweller with club-like claws that strike faster than any other animal on Earth; a favorite macro sighting.
species.population_info: Not formally assessed for conservation status; common in its burrows across the Indo-Pacific, though its secretive habits make it an infrequent sighting.

species.description: Fast, vividly green-and-pink wrasse darting constantly over shallow reef; one of the most common fish you'll see.
species.population_info: Least Concern and extremely abundant -- one of the very first fish you'll notice on almost any shallow Red Sea reef.

species.description: Comically cube-shaped fish, bright yellow with dark spots as a juvenile, that swims with tiny fins in a slow hover.
species.population_info: Least Concern and common throughout the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea; juveniles' bright yellow fades with age.

species.description: Bold, territorial Red Sea surgeonfish with electric blue-and-black striping, fiercely guarding its patch of shallow reef.
species.population_info: Least Concern; a Red Sea and Gulf of Aden specialty, extremely common and fiercely territorial on shallow reef flats.
